The $50 market find that sparked a 1000-piece vintage fashion obsession

Sydney Morning Herald June 06, 2026

Everything old is new again, with vintage clothing now a key element of the global fashion industry. Here, three local collectors reveal what drives their passion.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Once, you could find rare fashion items in the local op shop. But today, it’s unlikely you’ll discover a coveted designer label from the 1980s, ’90s and early noughties under a stack of old clothes dropped off at a charity store. Clothes from this era are now referred to collectively as “vintage”, and it’s become one of the strongest growth areas in fashion worldwide. Here, three Australian collectors discuss the thrill of building their vintage fashion treasure troves.

The founder of Déclic, a men’s clothing and accessories business in Melbourne and Sydney, has been immersed in fashion and design since he started his business in the late 1980s. His warehouse-style home in South Yarra, Melbourne, is filled with suits, shirts and hundreds of ties that capture the history of fashion through the decades.

The ties include those from New York designer Gene Meyer, along with Moschino, Hubert de Givenchy, Piero Fornasetti, Dolce & Gabbana and Hedi Slimane, with Slimane heralding the return of the narrow tie and silhouette for men in 2000. A knitted panelled shirt from Comme des Garçons from the early 1990s also appears in his collection, along with a pristine white shirt by Viktor & Rolf with its original swing tags. A rack of suits by Versace, Paul Smith and Zegna, also from this period, stands nearby, with many of the ties kept in a vintage suitcase or in boxes in the basement.

A Dolce & Gabbana tie from the early ’90s includes a racy image of a female from the 1950s, concealed on the tipping (the lining at the end). “When I was working, I’d always wear a suit and tie,” says Du Puy. “Now these pieces act as touchstones to my past as much as reflecting each period.”

He also recalls the impact that certain films had on fashion: “Remember Michael Douglas in Wall Street and the power image his character [Gordon Gekko in the late 1980s film] portrayed, as well as his brashness?” Pleated trousers, braces and wide ties all became popular as a result.

This overly confident attitude of “anything is possible” is reflected in the width (up to nine centimetres) of many of the ties displayed on the oak table in his own library. “Hedi Slimane made a similar impact with his narrow ties, ushering in a time of considerably more restraint,” he says.

While Du Puy has since sold Déclic, he still loves visiting great vintage stores in Paris. He sees the “thirst” of Parisian shoppers hunting for vintage pieces, including those from Maison Margiela. Stores, such as The Broken Arm in Haut-Marais, sell vintage Comme des Garçons with substantial price tags. “Often, these shirts from the 1980s are more expensive than the latest designs,” he says.

While the urge to buy has slightly subsided, he still enjoys returning home to Melbourne with a vintage shirt or tie. “They’re like art, but wearable art. It still feeds my creativity.”

Interior designer Sandy Geyer, who founded the Melbourne-based practice Geyer (now Geyer Valmont) with her partner Peter Geyer, could have easily chosen a career in fashion. In her teens, she would pore over Vogue patterns and make her own clothes.

Today, meticulous cataloguing in the bedroom of her Victorian terrace in Parkville, Melbourne, includes images of the shoes found in the 100 or so boxes that line her wall-to-wall wardrobe or are neatly stacked below the bed. The names on the boxes, along with the labels on her mainly black clothes, are a who’s who of the fashion world: Yohji Yamamoto, Comme des Garçons, Vivienne Westwood and Maison Martin Margiela, along with early designs from Thierry Mugler, Romeo Gigli and Jean Paul Gaultier.

When Geyer started working in the 1970s, she could afford to buy the latest fashion from the House of Merivale and Mr John. “The first thing I bought was an aqua, double-breasted fisherman’s rib cardigan, paid off in instalments,” she says. Later, other stores in Melbourne and Sydney, such as Masons, Saba, Trellini and Cose Ipanema, started to import Japanese and European fashion. A 1990s Martin Margiela wool coat, with its high collar, is still a favourite.

Geyer delights in presenting each piece and explaining its history, the cut and silhouette, as well as the fabric. She recalls going to Singapore for business during the ’90s and hunting down what was known as “The Gorilla Store”. Her route took her to an eight-storey housing estate with shops and other commercial uses at ground level.

“The roller door was shut and I had to wait for at least an hour,” Geyer recalls. The wait paid off when the first box opened revealed an organza shirt appliqued with oversized roses from the mid-1980s. She knew instinctively it was by Comme des Garçons. A pleated skirt with a boxy-shaped shirt, both from Yohji Yamamoto, are often worn with jewellery designed by Mari Funaki, one of Australia’s most revered contemporary jewellers.

For Geyer, clothing is an art form, as exemplified by her Yohji Yamamoto black leather handbag from the mid-1980s, one of only two in Australia and designed with its own pedestal. It sits on the bedroom ledge in front of a painting by Scottish artist Leon Morrocco. “I wouldn’t say that I am, or was, obsessed with chasing great clothes,” she says. “There’s that sense of exhilaration in purchasing something unique or a limited-edition piece and the feeling of wearing something so beautiful. It elevates the spirits.”

The owner of Cara Mia Vintage, Weinstock has been hunting for vintage clothes for almost 30 years. Her Mediterranean-style home in Sydney’s eastern suburbs includes a large space referred to as the “shop”, which is brimming with racks of clothing both for sale and for her own personal wardrobe – an estimated 1000 items between the two.

“Certain pieces move between both,” says Weinstock, whose personal collection includes a strong representation of Vivienne Westwood, including an impressive six corsets from the early 1990s. “I just sold a number of vintage pieces to a stylist who was searching for gowns for stars attending red-carpet events in Los Angeles.”

Weinstock, who studied media and communications before switching to law, and later followed her passion for vintage, recalls a “lightning bolt” moment when the “hunt” started. “I bought a Versace couture dress at the Rozelle collectors market when I was 16. From memory, it cost about $50.”

Her largest windfall was 10 years ago, when she came across a Melbourne woman selling vintage Yves Saint Laurent from the 1970s and ’80s on eBay on behalf of a friend. That stash comprised about 500 pieces, with most items unworn and with their original tags. Weinstock was told that many of the items, including bags and shoes, came from the iconic Georges department store in Collins Street, so she jumped on a plane to Melbourne that day. After the shock of the “great reveal”, she purchased the lot (a condition of the sale was that it be sold in its entirety), and shipped everything back to Sydney. “I still have a few pieces but Yves Saint Laurent designed for tall slim women and I’m shorter and curvier,” she says. “That [Melbourne collection] was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.”

She still receives calls, such as a recent one from a woman in Canberra who had been collecting designers, such as Chanel, for 40 years. In this instance, a trip resulted in a couple of Chanel suits from the 1990s and a few evening dresses from the ’60s and ’70s.

For Weinstock, as with many people addicted to vintage fashion, wearing vintage allows her to feel “special” and reflect her own personality.

“Vintage comes with a whole other life, a history. It’s also beautifully made.” For serious hunters of vintage, there’s always just one more purchase.

The fragrance trend that has shoppers wanting to smell like ‘a little treat’

Sydney Morning Herald June 06, 2026

Bergamot, sandalwood and essence of … cow? Don’t laugh, dairy fragrances are now on trend.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Cold milk. Fig milk. Coconut milk. No, this isn’t my grocery list for the week. Those are the scent notes on the bottles of perfumes I saw on a recent visit to my local cosmetics counter.

There’s You Soie by Glossier, which combines rice milk and bergamot; Angel Blush by Mugler, with almond milk and sandalwood; and First Milk by the Nue Co., packaged in a vessel resembling a milk bottle.

At a time when young people are lining up for specialty coffees and matcha lattes, it’s little surprise that savvy brands want to get in on the hype. Across culture, milk does seem to be on the mind: tradwives are extolling raw milk, and whole milk is once again near the top of the food pyramid in the United States after the Trump administration released new dietary guidelines this year.

Some fragrance makers have tied these scents to feelings of nostalgia and comfort. The Nue Co. describes the milky note in its perfume as “our first scent memory – the soft embrace of early connection”.

But hold on: what does milk really smell like? Not a lot, unless it’s spoiled. That’s why most of these scents draw on different aroma compounds known as lactones to evoke ideas like “creamy” and “soft” that people may unconsciously associate with milk. Fragrance experts say these milky scents also involve a bit of branding sleight of hand.

“If you think about Abercrombie & Fitch’s ‘Fierce’, it was such a great and huge fragrance, but nobody talked about what was in it,” said Vicken Arslanian, a long-time fragrance distributor and the owner of Commodity, a perfume brand whose offerings include “Milk” and the recently released “Milk Orchid”.

Arslanian said he and his colleagues at Commodity stumbled on the scent almost by accident. The brand began with a “hot and cold” concept that had elements of warm marshmallow and toasted sesame: “When we smelled it, we saw an image of milk,” he recalled.

Customers weren’t always so inquisitive about scent notes, he said. A fragrance was once more of what he called a “closed creation”. The ingredients and layers that made a perfume smell as it did were largely indistinguishable to the untrained nose.

“Today, because people have now a deep interest in fragrance, the best way for us to connect to it and to speak about it is through language, and food is one of those main languages,” Arslanian said.

“I can relate to ‘matcha’ much better than I can relate to ‘Iso E Super,’ ” he added, referring to a synthetic aroma molecule.

With trends such as the “clean girl aesthetic” and “no-make-up make-up” still in full force, the idea of a barely there milk scent may evoke the same natural, “I woke up like this” spirit.

Glossier, for instance, describes its new You Soie fragrance as “skin-scent enhancing.” And DedCool, a fragrance brand, has four milk-forward scents, -including one that’s meant to smell “familiar, like warm, clean skin”.

Minimalist, nearly odourless perfume grew popular over the past few years, as beauty became “more about optimisation than opulence,” as writer Rachel Syme put it in a New York Times column in 2018, writing about a wave of fragrances she termed “the New Softies”. But when lactone compounds are mingled with other notes – such as vanilla, fig, tonka bean – some of today’s milky scents are distinctly foodie.

“When I smell a milk fragrance, I get the satisfaction of a good meal, like there’s something that scratches the inside of my brain,” said Asia Grant, founder of Redoux, a bespoke fragrance house. “Whether it’s my amygdala or dopamine receptors or serotonin, whatever it is, it’s the same button that’s pressed after having ice-cream.”

Grant, who’s also the founder of Scent Social Club, a tour to various perfume stores in the Nolita neighbourhood of Manhattan, said she had received more requests for milk fragrances in recent weeks.

“The girls and the guys love smelling like a little treat,” she added.

According to Sue Chan, founder of Care of Chan, a creative agency that helps brands such as J. Crew and Aritzia host dinners and cocktail parties, the push of milk-scented perfumes points to how the fashion and beauty industries have embraced food to get in front of younger consumers.

“I think now that food, restaurant culture is so much a part of the zeitgeist, it would make sense that brands are continuing to use food as a vehicle to reach new audiences,” Chan said.

“Food is super accessible because we all have to eat three times or more a day, so everyone can align with and relate to food.”

Customers, she added, also seem to like finding food in unexpected places: in the Tomato Leaves soap by Loewe, for example, or in candles sculpted to look like tinned fish or a plate of spaghetti.

“Some of these food-related ones are a little bit irreverent and playful, which is appealing, especially in a time that’s so serious,” Chan said.

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

World Cup 2026: guide to all 1,248 players

The Guardian Thu, 04 Jun 2026 08:55:49 GMT

Everything you need to know (and more) about every squad member. Click on the player pictures for more information

Having squeezed in via the playoffs, Koubek’s well-drilled side have hopes of advancing from a middling group. Read the team guide here.

The spine of the side has plenty of experience, led by Soucek in midfield, while Schick scored 16 Bundesliga goals this season.

A serious lack of technical players, with the team relying too heavily on physicality, work rate, aggression and set pieces.

Everything the Guardian does – from in-depth and exhaustive guides like these to critical investigative reporting – is funded by the direct backing of readers who believe in independent journalism. If you don't already, please consider supporting us today.

Playing in a third World Cup on home soil, El Tri are competitive and flexible but may struggle to meet fans’ high expectations. Read the team guide here.

Flexible tactics, a tight defensive unit and an approach based on intensity, aggressive pressing and quick transitions.

Pressure as co-hosts could affect even an experienced squad, while Aguirre’s pragmatic approach has drawn criticism.

Bafana Bafana have emerged from a stagnant period after hosting in 2010 and held off Nigeria in qualifying. Read the team guide here.

International setup revitalised under Broos, knitted together by Mokoena in midfield, and built on well-drilled teamwork.

A squad mainly made up of domestic players lacks wider experience and will rely heavily on counterattacks to create chances.

The Taegeuk Warriors went unbeaten to qualify for their 11th straight finals, but ambitions do not extend far beyond escaping their group. Read the team guide here.

With a robust core, the team has a great spirit and a proper talisman in former Premier League golden boot winner Son.

Uncertainty over ideal formation, with a late switch to 3-4-3 during qualifying, plus fears about form and fitness of key players.

Surprise qualifiers who stunned Italy in the playoffs, Barbarez’s intense and unpredictable side could win over neutrals. Read the team guide here.

Aggressive defending, direct, passionate football and quick transitions, plus a huge young talent in Alajbegovic.

Intensity can go too far, with a loss of shape and discipline; unlikely to be able to dominate games in their group.

Marsch has turned the co-hosts into a solid and settled team, and worked to develop the mentality to handle pressure. Read the team guide here.

Consistent 4-4-2 approach built on pressing from the front and pace out wide, all backed by a resilient defensive unit.

Fitness fears over star man Davies, a competitive group and the burden of never having won a World Cup match.

The 2022 hosts stumbled through qualifying but could benefit from a much lower profile in these finals. Read the team guide here.

Hugely experienced coach Lopetegui will put hard focus on soaking up pressure and looking to hit opponents on the break.

Defence was a mess in qualifying, conceding 24 times in 10 games in the main section, while regional conflict badly disrupted preparation.

Yakin is aiming for the 'best World Cup from a Swiss team' as he seeks to turn reliable regulars into contenders this summer. Read the team guide here.

Comfortable in qualifying, topped their group with a mix of experience and fresh talent knitted together by Xhaka.

Some tactical uncertainty over formation, and big expectations from fans despite their side lacking depth beyond the starting XI.

Five-time champions have turned to Ancelotti, who has built an attacking side eager to end years of underachievement. Read the team guide here.

Built around Vinícius, the team has a solid spine which allows room for attacking flair in an aggressive 4-2-4 formation.

The full-backs do not match up to former greats, while 34-year-old Neymar may struggle to contribute fully due to injuries.

Grenadiers will be group outsiders after reaching their first World Cup since 1974 despite turmoil at home. Read the team guide here.

Migné has built a disciplined side with the pace and skill to counter effectively, with Bellegarde and Isidor bringing proven quality.

Instability has affected the team’s buildup, with key striker Nazon held up in Iran and Migné unable to visit the country he coaches.

Atlas Lions made history as Africa’s first semi-finalists in Qatar and expect to make a similar impact after a recent coaching change. Read the team guide here.

Ouahbi’s setup will create space for star player Hakimi, while reaching the last four in 2022 has boosted collective belief.

The Afcon hosts struggled to cope under pressure, culminating in a farcical final, and will be under close scrutiny again this summer.

Clarke’s side ended 28-year wait to qualify in cathartic style and will seek to reward travelling fans with a first trip to the knockouts. Read the team guide here.

Built around key lieutenants like McTominay and Robertson, Scotland’s first-choice XI is organised and hugely experienced.

The team lacks a reliable scorer, with Clarke often criticised for his caution, while Billy Gilmour’s injury will hurt a squad lacking depth.

At their sixth successive finals, the Socceroos arrive with an experienced core, young attacking talent and designs on a first knockout win. Read the team guide here.

Popovic improved the team in qualifying and has made them tougher to beat, while Irankunda leads a dangerous counterattacking unit.

The new coach is eager to shake off the ‘underdogs’ tag, but it may prove tough with a lack of high-profile names in a transitional squad.

Alfaro has rebuilt the team around 'Paraguayan DNA – intensity and clean sheets' and hopes of progress are high after 12 years away. Read the team guide here.

La Albirroja will rely on the assets that saw them through qualifying: playing a physical style with the tenacity to dig out unlikely results.

Only two teams scored fewer goals in Conmebol qualifying and there may be an over-reliance on Enciso to create and take chances.

After a remarkable 22-year absence following their third-place finish in 2002, Montella's talented squad are primed to make an impact on their return to the world stage. Read the team guide here.

Montella has built a harmonious squad with in-form players and two of Europe’s brightest attacking talents in the shape of Guler and Yildiz.

Lack of a proven striker and big-game experience in some areas increases the risk of the wheels coming off as they did at Euro 2020.

Expectations are low for the co-hosts after a turbulent buildup, but there is a path to the latter stages if Pochettino can harness his team’s abilities. Read the team guide here.

The core of the squad are ‘glue guys’ with prior World Cup experience, while their head coach knows how to win knockout matches.

Pochettino still seems unclear on his best team and tactical setup, leaving many home fans frustrated before a ball has been kicked.

The smallest nation by population and area to reach a World Cup, Advocaat’s side will seek to make a splash beyond their surprise qualification. Read the team guide here.

Advocaat’s return is a huge bonus; the vastly experienced head coach has led the team’s improvement and brought in players from the island’s diaspora.

The team’s possession-based style may need to be overhauled in a tough group, and kicking off against Germany is a particularly daunting test.

At their fifth World Cup, this may be El Tri’s strongest squad, seeking to win their first knockout game after qualifying in impressive fashion. Read the team guide here.

A defence marshalled by Pacho and Hincapié conceded just five goals in 18 qualifiers and Beccacece has introduced a Bielsa-esque pressing mentality.

Scoring remains a problem and beyond veteran striker Enner Valencia, attacking options are talented but raw and unproven at the highest level.

Winners in 2014, Die Mannschaft crashed out at the group stage in the last two finals but have rebuilt well under tactical obsessive Nagelsmann. Read the team guide here.

A blend of rising stars and reliable stalwarts, this squad has more than enough creative talent to take advantage of a decent group-stage draw.

This is not yet a vintage Germany side and results have been inconsistent, while Neuer is back in goal after a reliable successor could not be found.

The Elephants believe they can do what their golden generation failed to: reach the knockout stages, or as Faé has said: ‘Why not win it?’ Read the team guide here.

Faé’s defence is settled but still flexible and did not concede in qualifying, and the coach has a wealth of attacking talent at his disposal.

There are questions over midfield selection and their underwhelming Afcon defence has lowered previously high expectations this summer.

Perennial dark horses capable of causing shocks, impressive warm-up results have fuelled belief they can break new ground by reaching the quarter-finals. Read the team guide here.

Samurai Blue play as a cohesive unit, pressing from the front in Moriyasu’s settled system, and now have the squad depth to make a deeper run.

Injury to Kaoru Mitoma is a blow and they have landed in a tough group with three experienced and physical opponents.

Koeman has been set a target of reaching the semi-finals, but has been forced to prioritise strength and fitness over skill with a raft of injury issues. Read the team guide here.

The Oranje smashed in 27 goals to qualify unbeaten, but it is their back four which looks most impressive on paper, marshalled by captain Van Dijk.

Several key players have suffered from injury layoffs or lack of game time this season, and facing Japan first will test this team’s cohesion.

Took two points from 18 in a disastrous qualifying campaign, but grasped their playoff chance under Potter and have the attacking talent to go further. Read the team guide here.

Potter has two elite finishers at his disposal up front but will set up with a hard-working back five to complement the firepower in his squad.

Isak endured a grim first season at Liverpool, and Potter has had limited time to apply his methods after taking over last October.

After six World Cups and six group-stage exits, the Eagles of Carthage seek to break new ground with an imposing team drawn from the country’s diaspora. Read the team guide here.

Did not concede a goal in qualifying and have been tactically flexible under Lamouchi, who has pleased supporters with his desire to bring young talent through.

Burnley’s Mejbri is the creative star of a low-key team lacking elite experience, who may find it difficult to play with freedom in a challenging group.

A time of transition for the Red Devils. Qualifying went smoothly but was never particularly eye-catching. Read the team guide here.

De Bruyne, Doku and Lukaku offer a serious attacking edge, though the latter played only 64 minutes for Napoli this season.

The defence is, except for Courtois, the weak point with the golden generation of Alderweireld, Kompany, Vermaelen and Vertonghen long gone.

Salah led the way through qualifying but limitations of the side were exposed at Afcon, where Senegal inflicted a semi-final defeat. Read the team guide here.

Cohesive, often hard to score against and emotionally committed.

Can look blunt if opponents double up on Salah and the midfield cannot pass through the press.

Smooth sailing in qualifying – anything but easy since then. The conflict with the United States threw their involvement into doubt but Ghalenoei's side are all set to compete. Read the team guide here.

Capable of mixing things up – in March friendlies they played a 3-6-1 against Nigeria and a 4-4-2 against Costa Rica.

Ghalenoei and his staff will have to work hard to minimise disruption for the squad, which will be based in Mexico but will play three group games in the US.

The All Whites are the lowest-ranked team at the tournament but the squad has evolved from part-timers to professionals. Read the team guide here.

There's no shortage of optimism – within the camp there's belief they can to make the knockout rounds for the first time.

Star striker Wood has had an injury-plagued 2026 and recent friendly results have been mixed at best.

An eclectic group of players, the Blue Sharks are swimming in completely uncharted waters as they make their World Cup debut. Read the team guide here.

A settled squad has been together for the best part of half a decade. Physical and happy to defend but blessed with technical forwards too.

Key defender Logan Costa has been out with an anterior cruciate ligament injury all season

The Green Falcons have had a chaotic buildup to the tournament, with Donis taking charge in April after the bitter exit of Hervé Renard.

Expectations are low, so to some extent the pressure is off. Expect Donis to focus his efforts on defensive solidity.

The team looks toothless up front: just seven goals were scored in 10 games in the main round of qualification.

Rightly among the favourites. De la Fuente has the perfect blend of youth and experience, prodigious talent and maturity.

Lamine Yamal and Williams have injected freshness into a team that still dominates the ball. The frontline will be hard to contain.

Are there any? The back four can have its moments but this is simply a fiercely competitive and united team.

The quarter-finals are the aim, but the buildup has been anything but smooth. Bielsa has been under pressure since a 5-1 loss to the USA in November.

Brace yourselves for Bielsa-ball: expect La Celeste to press their opponents high up the field and chase the ball at all times.

Uruguay do not have the scoring power of old. Hopes are being pinned on Darwin Núñez, who has struggled for form at Al-Hilal.

France have attacking talents that are the envy of the world. But will Deschamps take the handbrake off and let them shine?

The front four is a remarkable quartet, and the back four isn't bad either. Their bench might be the strongest at the tournament.

A cynic might suggest the head coach's conservatism. More accurately, it's the challenge he faces in putting all the puzzle pieces together.

After a marathon journey to get here (they played 21 qualifiers, more than anyone else) Arnold's side are out to prove they belong on the world stage.

As Arnold says, the pressure is on the other three teams in the group. Iraq have nothing to lose.

Not exactly free-scoring. Breaking down three tough defences in the group will be a huge challenge.

Golden generation vibes for Haaland and friends. But expect Solbakken's side to prioritise effectiveness over aesthetics.

Haaland will be eager to grab this opportunity on the world stage. The team averaged nearly five goals a game in qualifying.

Tough group means they have to hit the ground running. First-choice goalkeeper has barely played for his club this season.

The Lions of Teranga arrive in North America in fine shape, thanks to a freshened-up frontline and a defence that is its usual sturdy self. Read the team guide here.

Thiaw has developed a more flexible tactical approach, while speed in attack will cause teams plenty of problems.

Recent tournament record, aside from the most recent Cup of Nations, is unimpressive.

One of this World Cup’s great unknowns. Qualifying was a cakewalk – but against generally poor opposition. Read the team guide here.

The squad boasts plenty of technical ability and Afcon highlighted just how good they can be at their best.

The Afcon quarter-final collapse against Nigeria remains fresh in minds. Was it an aberration or a sign of how this team performs under pressure?

World Cup and Copa América holders travel with a squad of familiar faces but perhaps not with players in peak physical condition.

Almost all of the class of 2022 is still around, including Messi.

Several players had injury setbacks at the end of very demanding seasons with their clubs.

Rangnick's high-pressing unit know exactly who they are. This is a side built not on stardom but on familiarity, trust and collective movement.

Continuity: Austria’s plan has been remarkably stable for years. Rangnick has had time to imprint his ideas.

If the structure slips even slightly, the aggressive counter-pressing approach can leave them exposed. Pre-tournament injury to Christoph Baumgartner is a huge blow.

A first finals appearance for a team who qualified with a match to spare. Will likely sit deep in a back five.

Will look to exploit quick transitions and the pace of star winger Mousa Al-Taamari.

Injury has ruled out key striker Yazan A-Naimat, leaving a huge hole in attack. Big-game experience is in short supply.

Experienced squad endured a rollercoaster qualifying campaign, beating Brazil and Argentina but losing to a poor Bolivia side.

Goals shouldn't be a problem. Suárez is coming off a prolific season in Portugal with Sporting and only Argentina scored more in Conmebol qualifying.

Tournament football leaves no room for the inconsistency that has become a hallmark of this side.

Pragmatic, detail-obsessed coach has the Leopards purring, with a united squad built around a clear collective identity.

Extremely difficult to break down and mentally tough as they come. Resilience defined their qualification campaign.

Rarely dominate games and struggle to create freely in open play. Preparations have been disrupted by Ebola outbreak in country.

One last hurrah for Ronaldo but last year's Nations League winners have quality throughout and lofty ambitions.

The core of the team is settled and the options varied and versatile. A squad still mourning Diogo Jota have a personal, collective mission.

Few and far between but there's always a risk of Ronaldo's outsized influence becoming a problem.

A historic first World Cup beckons. Cannavaro has stuck with the 5-2-3 system that powered the White Wolves through qualifying.

Qualification was built off a solid defence that includes Khusanov, with just seven goals conceded in 10 games.

Cannavaro was a legend as a player but his managerial career has been mixed. Goals are likely to be a problem.

Semi-finalists in 2018 and 2022. Likely to revert to a back four after recent wing-back experiment brought mixed results

Bags of experience and, as past World Cups have shown, a winning mentality. Modric remains a midfield maestro.

Can the old guard still cut it? All that experience means plenty of miles in the legs and sapping temperatures ahead.

Cruised through qualifying but the opposition was hardly taxing. So it's the usual question: how will they fare when they come up against the best in a knockout tie?

They have enviable attacking options, a host of No 10s and in Rice one of the best midfielders in the world.

There are question marks over the defensive options and, as ever, fitness concerns over key players.

A team littered with attacking talent that cruised through qualifying but their recent run of defeats is a concern.

Have developed into a major threat from set pieces and in Semenyo the Black Stars have one of the most in-form attackers in European club football.

Lack of elite defenders is a worry and goalkeeping unit lacks international experience.

La Marea Roja are hopeful of improving upon hapless 2018 showing after long development under former Leeds coach.

Squad has been together a long time, has pace and is full of confidence. Solid recent showings in Gold Cup and Nations League.

Tend to struggle against the bigger teams and several key players are now well into their 30s.

A favourite in the Czech national team since last autumn. In the space of a few days he helped seal two play-off successes via penalty shootouts. Before then he had only saved one spot-kick in domestic football, but he excelled in the scrap for a World Cup spot like nobody else in the Czech squad. “It feels like a dream,” he said after the wins over Republic of Ireland and Denmark. Kovar is a huge talent, calm by nature and mostly phlegmatic. As a teenager, he left a small Czech town to join Manchester United. He has since won three league titles in three different countries: Czechia, Germany and the Netherlands. Although he’s usually quiet and modest, he thrives in the big moments and coaches joke that he brings luck. “It wasn’t any great luck, I simply did my homework,” he said while the whole country was lauding him. Still, speculation persists over whether he will be the first-choice goalkeeper for the World Cup.

Zima can come across as a rather unusual young man, especially in his public appearances. At first glance, you cannot tell what kind of day he’s having. After the first question, you still don’t know how the interview will go. Zima – meaning “winter” – is not a flashy star, despite the fact his career quickly took off as a teenager. At 19, with just 156 minutes in the domestic league, he was signed by Slavia Prague from Sigma Olomouc for more than €1m, a fee rarely seen in Czech football for such a player. The move did not faze him. “I have no reason to be nervous,” he said. “The pitch is always the same size. Opponents don’t scare me.” A year and a half later, he moved to Italy for four times that fee, joining Torino. In January 2024, he returned to Slavia Prague to restart his career and, at €4m, became the most expensive signing in Czech league history. Now a four-time domestic league champion, he is widely praised for his precise approach to defending, though critics still say he can be too laid back, and prone to defensive lapses.

Fans of human anatomy should take a look at Tomas: the centre-back has what may well be the biggest calves at the tournament. He’s not particularly tall, but is pure muscle. He’s also one of the most experienced players in the Czech squad and is a quiet leader at Slavia Prague, where he has won four league titles, the latest as captain. He comes from a region where cross-country skiing is more common than football but fell in love with the game competing with his two brothers. With no proper pitch in his village, he used to cycle three miles to training. Through consistency and hard work, Holes has gradually developed into a leader without ever acting like a superstar. Despite Czechia being a largely secular country, he is a devout evangelical Christian and says: “Faith is the most important thing for me, apart from my family. I often feel like guardian angels help me on the pitch.” Away from the pitch, Holes enjoys the quiet life with his two daughters, often going fishing and reading history books before bed.

Hranac grew up in a small town in western Czechia, far from major academies – so when his talent became clear, that had to change. At 14, he travelled 60 miles to a boarding school in Plzen while his parents worked across the border in Germany. The sacrifices paid off. These days he has a calm and reserved exterior, and can appear shy, but that disguises the real fight and passion inside him. ”Robin takes a lot of hits but never reacts or gets angry,” says his dad. “He has an extremely high pain threshold.” After just one impressive season in the Czech league he broke into the national team, marked Cristiano Ronaldo at Euro 2024, and earned an €8m move to Hoffenheim in 2024. Best deployed in the middle of a back three.

Long overlooked due to his slight build, Coufal was told at 17 by coaches at Czech club Banik Ostrava that he would never make a living from football. He was quick and determined, but too small and easily outmuscled in duels. At that time, he hated football. “But I promised myself I’d prove them all wrong. I’m a bit of a madman who likes chasing his dreams,” he said. True recognition only came at 26, when he was signed by Slavia Prague and went on to win three consecutive league titles before making a surprise move to the Premier League. “At first I thought they had the wrong name. Why would they sign a veteran?” he joked of his move to West Ham. In London he enjoyed a fairytale spell, culminating in winning the Europa Conference League. But after five years he found himself on the periphery with the Hammers. Again, though, he refused to give up. Now 33, he has rebuilt his career at Hoffenheim and is playing arguably his best football.

One of the breakout stars of the recent Czech league season, one of the country’s best out-and-out defenders and a champion with Slavia, Chaloupek’s performances were such that he attracted interest from Roma and Fiorentina in January. A year earlier, however, he wasn’t even in the starting lineup after a tough time with injury. He’s a hard-working, disciplined and reliable defender – a nightmare for attackers due to his uncompromising style. Off the pitch, he is quiet and reserved. Had football not worked out, he says he might have become a police officer. “I liked the idea of being fair, principled and standing up for the truth,” he says. Chaloupek was born with a cleft palate and underwent surgery at the age of three. “I was mocked by other kids because of it. It was hard, but it made me stronger.” He later considered plastic surgery as he still breathes through only one nostril.

Krejci’s childhood dream of playing in the Premier League turned into something of a nightmare last season as Wolves endured defeat after defeat, suffering relegation to the Championship. The centre-back, however, has quickly – and to the surprise of some – turned into one of Rob Edwards’ most valuable players. Over the past four years, his rise has been rapid. He won two league titles with Sparta Prague, became the most expensive signing in Girona’s history, before a loan to the Premier League last summer. Krejci follows a simple motto: ”If you feel you should do, decide or change something, don’t hesitate. No one else will do it for you.” He used to struggle with discipline and picked up too many yellow cards. Yet since March, he has been captain of the national team and led with distinction, scoring in the playoff games against Republic of Ireland and Denmark. “I believed in myself because I know what I can do,” said the 27-year-old.

An unassuming character, when Darida played for Freiburg from 2013 to 2015 he rode a scooter to training. He got rid of it when he moved to Berlin with Hertha, though. “It wasn’t really safe in Berlin traffic,” he said. “My father took it back to Czechia and I gave it to my sister.” It wasn’t an easy journey into professional football: he almost had to quit the game when he was 16 when his growth stopped, leaving him struggling to handle the physicality of the game. But, via hard work and a gluten-free diet, he developed the strength needed. He spent seven years at Hertha before moving to Aris in Greece in 2022, and returning to Czechia last year with Hradec Kralove. He brings huge experience, having made his international debut back in 2012, and captained the team at Euro 2020. After that tournament he retired from international football, saying: “I experienced beautiful moments in the national team, but now, I’d like to spend much more time with my family and my young son.” But he was tempted back in March this year, returning, aged 35, to help them in the World Cup qualification play-offs.

A real talent, who could make a big impact. Hlozek has played in Germany since 2022 when Bayer Leverkusen took note of his record at Sparta Prague: a senior debut at 16, scoring 40 goals and making 36 assists in 132 games, and winning the Czech Cup. He joined for an initial €13m, but only stayed for two years, having grown frustrated with a rotational role, moving to Hoffenheim for an initial €17m. Hugely versatile, he’s a threat out wide or through the middle. He’s a big fan of tattoos, with a giant lion on his left thigh. “It has a deep, personal meaning for me and gives me strength,” he said last year. “Leo is my star sign and I identify with the animal. The lion is known for its fighting mentality, exudes an aura and is the king of the wilderness. It took five and a half hours in the first sitting, then we took a break and after that it was another five and a half hours. But I'm happy that I got through it. I like it a lot."

Schick’s goalscoring gift was obvious from a very young age. Playing for Vestec, a village near Prague, he didn’t celebrate his goals, said coaches, but would instead just pick the ball up, take it to the centre circle and ask for the game to be resumed. When he missed a big chance, he would cry and had to be substituted. Aged eight he was inspired by watching Wayne Rooney play for Manchester United at Sparta Prague. He recalled: “I thought that I want to do this – never get a normal job, and earn a living like him.” It worked out well. He played a grand total of 36 league minutes in Sparta Prague’s first team before Sampdoria decided they had seen enough, paying €4m for the gangly 20-year-old. He signed for Roma a year later in a move that could have been worth up to a club record €42m, but it didn’t really work out there: he ended up on the wing, was loaned to Leipzig, then was sold to Leverkusen in 2020 for €26.5m - which is where everything clicked. In April this year, he scored his 100th goal for them in all competitions. He helped Czechia qualify for the first time in 20 years via the playoffs. He was 10 when they last played at a World Cup. “I vividly remember the games. The Czech fans have waited a long time for this.”

An experienced forward who made his senior debut for Slavia Prague back in 2016, and now, a decade later, turns out for rivals Sparta. Kuchta also had spells in Russia with Lokomotiv Moscow and Denmark with Midtjylland. Life with the international side hasn’t always been easy: in November 2023 he was one of three players – with Jakub Brabec and Vladimir Coufal – kicked out of the training camp for going clubbing two days before a Euro 2024 qualifier against Moldova. Aggressive and powerful on the pitch, he’s more nurturing off it, raising chickens, rabbits, ducks and geese at his family farm. When he moved to Moscow in 2022 and had to leave them behind he said: "Chickens are part of my life, I was used to going to them in the morning, then again after training, it cleared my head. It will take a while to adjust. I can’t take them there, it’s -17 degrees… The chickens will just have to wait until I am home, and I will pay a lot of attention to them again."

Cousin of teammate David Doudera, Cerv made his international debut two years ago, soon after joining Viktoria Plzen from Slovan Liberec, and was the only newcomer in the national side’s Euro 2024 squad. He wasn’t expecting the call when it came. “I didn’t really believe it at first,” he said after arriving at the team’s training camp. “I went on vacation, so when I got the call I had to ​​leave my family there and fly away. I left them there to enjoy the warmth and sunshine. And here we are in the rain and fog. But it's really incredible." Settling in as part of the national set-up wasn’t too hard, though: “I know a lot of guys from the Under-21s and I have Doudis [Doudera], my cousin, and the guys from Plzen here, so everything is fine. But I'm probably hanging out with Doudis most.” Two years on and he’s fully integrated, and an experienced, reliable option for this World Cup squad. His surname translates as “worm”.

A tall, experienced option up front, Chytil made quite a splash on his international debut in 2022 - scoring a ten-minute hattrick in a friendly against the Faroe Islands. He’s known for being physical and fearless, a real handful, and could be an important weapon this summer. He spent most of his early career at Sigma Olomouc before 2023’s move to Slavia Prague where, again, he had a scoring debut, netting against Hradec Králové on the opening day. The club’s manager, Jindrich Trpisovsky, described him well: “The first thing that comes to mind about Mojmir is the wider benefit he brings to the team: his fighting spirit, his annoyingness for defenders. He has very good ball coverage, perhaps the best back-to-goal game in the league. He is a team player, combative, with excellent physical qualities.”

When Jurasek moved from Slavia Prague to Benfica for €14m three years ago, becoming one of the Czech league’s most expensive exports, it seemed Czech football would finally have a full-back at a top European club. His father even flew to Portugal by private jet for the signing ceremony, as Benfica set his release clause at a whopping €80m, an indication of the regard in which they held him. However, a serious ankle injury disrupted his progress, and he lost his place in the Benfica first team. Jurasek rebuilt his career during a loan spell at Hoffenheim, before returning to Slavia in January. “I just hope I don’t bring bad luck,” he confessed before helping them to the league title – the first title success of his career. With a strong left foot, excellent stamina and acceleration, a big physical presence and a great crossing ability, Jurasek has just about every attribute you would want from a left-back.

Widely linked with a big move after this tournament – this summer is a real chance for Sulc to showcase his talents. Soon after being voted the best Czech player of 2025 he joined Lyon from Viktoria Plzen for an initial €7.5m, handed the formidable task of filling the void left behind by Rayan Cherki. But he shrugged off that pressure and stepped up with some superb displays, earning plenty of praise from supporters. The reception surprised him. “It’s been incredible,” he said in April. “Honestly, I didn't expect so much love from fans or that it would happen so quickly … It’s my first experience in one of the top five leagues in Europe, and the football in Czechia is simply much less demanding. The coach has been brilliant with me.” He’s happy to be versatile, too. “I'll always do my best, even if they put me as a centre-back!”

Stanek has never got anything for free in his career. He started out as an ice hockey player and was a promising forward, a talent he inherited from his father. But he chose to leave the ice in pursuit of a football career and went straight from Sparta to England, where he was a backup goalkeeper at Everton, facing shots from Romelu Lukaku, Kevin Mirallas and Samuel Eto’o in training. “I felt like I was in another world. I was taking a battering, but I didn’t want to give up,” he later recalled. He dreamed of following in the footsteps of compatriot Petr Cech, but had to take the long way round. He even spent a season in the Czech third division to build his confidence. ”In hindsight, I feel like a cat with seven lives,” he said of his nomadic career. “That’s why when I go to the zoo, I spend most of my time with the tigers. I look for inspiration in them.” He eventually settled with Viktoria Plzen, where his career took off, leading to a move to Slavia Prague in 2024.

An imposing 1.88m presence out wide, he is pacy as well. Provod rose through the ranks at hometown club Viktoria Plzen, then had a series of loans as he established himself, first at Banik Sokolov, then Ceske Budejovice and finally Slavia Prague, whom he joined on a permanent deal in 2020. “It feels unbelievable,” he said when he signed, “it feels like a beautiful story. It all happened really fast. It’s a great challenge for me, and I did not hesitate. Slavia is the biggest and most successful club in Czechia, so it was clear immediately.” He made his international debut the same year in a Nations League game against Slovakia. He missed Euro 2020 due to injury, but made the squad for 2024 and scored in the opener against Portugal. A versatile performer, he could also be called upon to do a job more centrally, or up front.

At 16, Sadilek made a bold move. Instead of following his older brother Lukas through the academy system in his home country, he left for the Netherlands, joining PSV. Maybe the time apart did them good. “As kids we were together every day,” remembered Michal, “and sometimes like all little boys we got on each other's nerves, fought and the like.” But these days they couldn’t be closer. “I’m proud of my brother. We write to each other after every match, and when there's a chance, we talk about everything.” He moved to Twente in 2022 for three years, before returning home with Slavia in 2025. His international career hasn’t been without its ups and downs: he made his debut in 2021 but had to pull out of the Euro 2024 squad after injuring his leg when he fell off his tricycle at the training camp. The FA said the incident happened when he drove the three-wheeled bike through a pothole and crashed, but they didn’t criticise him. “The accident happened in the player's free time, which he was allowed to spend as he pleased. He did not violate team rules or other internal agreements."

A 1.98m powerhouse who isn’t afraid of getting stuck in. In January he embraced his bad boy image, saying: “People don’t like me? That actually makes me feel good.” But in May things reached a tipping point: he was sent off for elbowing an opponent in the head in a chaotic Prague derby, his third red of the season, prompting Slavia’s furious chairman, Jaroslav Tvrdik, to transfer-list him. “Tomas is clearly unable to control his behaviour,” said Tvrdik. “With this behaviour, he does not belong on the field.” The league’s disciplinary committee banned him for six games, saying the elbow was “not an accidental event … neither emotions nor the assertive style of play that Tomas Chory presents can be an excuse for such an action”. He has plenty of experience, and has spent his whole club career in Czechia apart from a loan spell in Belgium with Zulte Waregem. He made his international debut in 2023, scoring and assisting in a 3-0 Euro 2024 qualifying win over Moldova.

One of the select few footballers who fans have forgiven for playing for both rival Prague clubs. An easy-going character, Zeleny is in no way a rebel or troublemaker, but he can be impatient, particularly when driving his car. “It annoys me when someone dawdles at the lights because they are on their phone,” he says. “That’s when I lean on the horn. Otherwise, I’m calm. People say you need to be ruthless in top football, but it’s not in my nature.” Zeleny is unlikely to change his nature now as he approaches his 34th birthday. He has never left the Czech league, making over 300 appearances since his debut for Hradec Kralove in 2010. Earlier in his career, he may have lacked the courage to move abroad; now he’s nearing the end of his time as an evergreen of Czech football. Fittingly, his surname translates to “green” in English.

Like his Slavia teammate Tomas Chory, Doudera had a lively Prague derby in May, with both shown red cards as the game descended into a mess of crowd violence. Doudera’s red was for abusing the referee; Slavia’s chairman, Jaroslav Tvrdik, responded by transfer-listing him. The defender later apologised, writing online: "I'm sorry for the whole situation. To the fans, to the whole of Slavia, to Czech football. These things shouldn't happen in a civilised world.” He now has a chance to redeem himself this summer. He made his international debut in 2023, a year after his move to Slavia. He said soon afterwards: “My dad and I always say that my story is worth a book. But I don't want to brag about it, it's just that I have it in me. Each of us has a story and everyone got here somehow. I wasn't a great talent from a young age. I was never in the youth national teams … I'm proud of myself for what I've accomplished.” Teammate Lukas Cerv is his cousin.

It wasn’t an easy season for Soucek as West Ham struggled, but he remains a fundamental part of Miroslav Koubek’s national side – a brilliantly energetic 1.93m force in midfield. Last year he was named Czech Footballer of the Year for the fourth time. He was brought up in Havlickuv Brod, a town with a population of 23,000 people, and comes from a sporting family: his dad a football coach and his mum a runner. “She runs half-marathons and marathons and sometimes when I was younger I went with her to the forest,” he says. “And sometimes when I was in pre-season I would go with her to run in the forest. I think I got my stamina from her.” Last year he published his autobiography, in which he revealed he had considered retiring early during what were “two years of horror” spent with insomnia and depression. He improved with medical help, and said his trademark “helicopter” goal celebration rose from the experience: “From match to match, I focused mainly on not sleeping, which actually disturbed me doubly. And that’s why the helicopter was created, my goal celebration. I start to spin slightly and enjoy the feeling of taking off. I like it when fans call me a helicopter. It’s a symbol of what I’ve done, what I’ve overcome, and where I am. It expresses my inner feeling that I can fight.”

Hornicek has spent roughly a third of his life in Portugal, where he moved aged 17. He was based in a boarding school 1,500 miles from home and was homesick, but never gave up his dream of a career in football. “That decision took away part of the youth I could have spent with friends, but I followed my dream. Even if I could turn back time, I wouldn’t change it,” he says. Nicknamed “Horny Czech“ in Portugal because of the difficulty of pronouncing his surname, he’s now a rising star in Czech goalkeeping. He started in Braga’s youth team and spent two years as a backup, before a spectacular breakthrough last season. He kept a clean sheet every other match and became known for saving penalties in the Europa League. Boasting high levels of concentration, he has improved his distribution and work on the ball in Portugal and has even been linked with Real Madrid of late. “It’s a shame my grandfather didn’t live to see [this]. He was my biggest supporter,” he says.

Raised in a footballing family. Sojka’s dad Jindrich was chairman of SK Klatovy for over 20 years, and his older brother plays for them now. Alexandr has gone the furthest in the family, though. He returned to his first club, Viktoria Plzen, this year when they activated a buy-back clause, re-signing him from Hradec Kralove. “We decided to activate the option," said the club’s sporting director, Martin Vozábal. "The goal is to increase competition in midfield and he performed very well during the autumn.” He has proved himself as a technically-gifted, versatile performer. His international inclusion was an overwhelming moment for his dad. "The whole family lives for it,” Jindrich told iSport. “The only pity is that his grandfather, a big fan of Plzen since childhood, did not live to see it. Sasa [Alexandr] is finally showing what is in him. People in this region live for football and they appreciate that a boy from Klatovy can reach such a level."

The baby of the squad, Sochurek was still 17 when the final selection was announced. A product of Sparta’s academy, he made his club debut last year, and his international debut in a warm-up game against Kosovo in May. But his cool, fearless approach convinced the coach, Miroslav Koubek, he was ready. After his first-team breakthrough at Sparta, coach Brian Priske said: “He plays like he's over 30. The first-team players immediately took him in and when they saw what he could do with the ball.” Sochurek’s youth coach Pavel Drsek told Eurofotbal. cz in May: “He's made a huge improvement in the last year, he’s grown bigger, he has strong thighs, it's hard to get him off the ball. He’s not a typical Czech midfielder, he likes the ball, his first thought is to go forward … And he's a great guy, a pure soul, but quiet. Once I handed him the captain's armband before a match and he immediately told me that he could not be the captain. He is not a classic leader, but he is clearly a driving force.”

A promising young winger who knew what he wanted from the moment he first kicked a ball. “I first played in the village where I was born, for AFK Horin, at the age of three,” he recalled. “Then we moved and I started playing for Melník. When I was six, we played a tournament somewhere, I don't know where exactly, and Slavia Prague scouted me there. So I went to Slavia for a trial and joined them when I was six.” He made rapid progress, and last year signed for Viktoria Plzen from Slovan Liberec. Viktoria’s sporting director, Daniel Kolar, called him “an extraordinary talent, which he confirmed in the Liberec jersey. Despite his still young age, he has already played almost 80 league matches. We have a clear development plan with him and we intend to push his potential even further.” Technically gifted, he has pace and an eye for goal – a useful option this summer. Models himself on Kevin De Bruyne.

Putellas doubles up to lead Spain rout and leave England staring at playoffs

The Guardian Fri, 05 Jun 2026 21:07:21 GMT

Spain 4-0 England

Guijarro 19, Putellas 37 55, Pina 78

Only a minor miracle will save European champions England from having to come through World Cup qualifying playoffs after they suffered an utterly humiliating 4-0 defeat by World Cup holders Spain in Mallorca.

A loss by only a one-goal deficit would have been enough to keep England’s hopes of topping their qualifying group alive after an immaculate campaign prior to this. However, with the head-to-head record between the top two sides coming into play should they finish level on points, this emphatic win, with talismanic Alexia Putellas scoring two, means Spain just need to beat Iceland on Tuesday to secure top spot at England’s expense.

Frankly, they deserve it. Sonia Bermúdez’s team didn’t just beat England, they annihilated them, dominating possession, with over 61% of the ball across the 90 minutes, and ensuring a beleaguered England stayed camped in their half, accruing 39 touches in the opposition box to England’s paltry seven.

It was always going to be a big ask to get a win away from home against the Spaniards, but hopes of a 1-0 defeat, to match the reverse fixture, or even a draw, to put England in a favourable position in Group A3 going into the final round of games on Tuesday were shattered in the first half.

England weren’t bad, not for the first 15 minutes at least, but there was a sloppiness to their play, a lack of sharpness demonstrative of a match coming almost three weeks after the end of the WSL season. That is no excuse for top professionals though, even if Spain’s domestic campaign concluded last weekend and were boosted by a Barcelona contingent buoyed by a fourth Champions League title.

It was a moment of magic inside 20 minutes that gave the home team a critical lead, Mallorca-born Guijarro capitalised on Lucy Bronze’s errant pass and drove forward, nutmegging Georgia Stanway on the way with zero impact on her momentum, before sending a low strike in from 25 yards which took a deflection off Esme Morgan to wrongfoot Hannah Hampton.

The celebrations were emphatic and Guijarro’s drive and strike were laced with the fury of not having been given a free-kick for what she believed was a foul on her moments prior.

The goal rattled Sarina Wiegman’s side, who only had one touch in the opposition box to Spain’s 18 in the first 45 minutes and had Salma Paralluelo been more clinical they could have been punished further sooner. Spain’s second arrived in the 36th minute and it was poor from England. Alex Greenwood was completely out of sync with the rest of the Lionesses’ back line, playing Putellas onside as she sprung clear on the left before sending a ferocious strike at Hampton. The Chelsea goalkeeper got her hands to it but failed to stop it from looping backwards and over across the goalline. She should have done better, but so should Greenwood, and so should so many in white shirts throughout the evening.

Bronze had said in the buildup that Spain “bring out the best in us” and that the rivalry had made them both better. At the Estadi Mallorca Son Moix there was little evidence of the best being brought out of England.

There was more sloppiness on display for Spain’s third, right-back Ona Batlle outpaced Lauren James, who slipped at the byline, before she cut back for Putellas, the forward’s effort was blocked on the line by Bronze, the ball came off the post and slipped between the legs of Greenwood and Putellas was alert, and she dived forward and turned it in.

It was a humbling goal to concede and changes came soon after, with Chloe Kelly and Beth Mead on for James and Ella Toone. Alessia Russo moved into the 10 in place of Toone as a result and, with no established centre-forward on the bench, Aggie Beever-Jones left out of the matchday squad as a selection decision, according to Wiegman, Lauren Hemp moved centrally with the newcomers either side of her. The impact was minimal though and it was Spain’s subs that would deliver. The large home crowd had enjoyed the show in Palma and they had further reason to celebrate in the 78th minute when, moments after coming on, the substitute Aitana Bonmatí found fellow sub Clàudia Pina and the forward shifted to the right of Arsenal centre-back Lotte Wubben-Moy and fired in.

England were bruised and Spain were showboating at the close. Turning the screw against the team that had the better of them just under 12 months prior in the Euro 2025 final. England looked like a shell of the side that earned that historic win, and a shell of the side that earned the 1-0 win in the reverse fixture in April.

England’s only key absentee due to injury is captain Leah Williamson too. As a result, an intense post-mortem will be needed following such a difficult defeat. Turning things around in time for the World Cup next summer, if they make it, through the playoffs, will be a huge job.

Tuchel confident ‘sharp’ Kane is in perfect form to lead England at World Cup

The Guardian Fri, 05 Jun 2026 20:53:05 GMT

Head coach says Bayern Munich striker is in ‘top shape’

England face New Zealand in warm-up on Saturday

Thomas Tuchel has said that Harry Kane is in top shape and ready to lead England to glory at the World Cup. The Bayern Munich striker has been short of fitness at previous major tournaments but he has enjoyed a brilliant season in Germany and has looked in peak physical condition in training this week.

England have prepared for the intense heat expected at the World Cup by heading to Florida to acclimatise to the weather and have been working in testing conditions at their pre-tournament base in West Palm Beach.

Tuchel is focused on recovery and knows that the team’s hopes of glory will rest heavily on Kane staying injury-free. The country’s record goalscorer remains a talismanic figure, despite struggling for form and fitness at Euro 2024, and has the backing of his manager before England cross Florida to face New Zealand in Tampa in their first warm-up game on Saturday.

“He looks in top shape,” Tuchel said. “He looks lean, sharp and he trains at the highest level. We had a defensive training session today and he was leading the intensity. He is so used to the high press from Bayern Munich and the intensive game that they play in the opponents’ half. He is leading by example. I think he is in the best shape.

“He is ready to go. We don’t have to be worried about him at all, even if it is hot in June. He has showed me the whole week that he is ready. He is our key player.”

The New Zealand game will kick off at 4pm local time (9pm BST), when the temperature is forecast to be 32C and the humidity levels at about 40%. Tuchel intends to play two different lineups in each half at the Raymond James Stadium and is focused on building his side’s energy levels.

“Some of them need a load, some of them need a recovery,” the German said. “We give 45 to everyone. We will try to keep Harry fit and play him as much as possible but hopefully we will have the chance to not need to play him every match 90 or 120 minutes.”

Tuchel indicated that Ollie Watkins will be Kane’s understudy, with Ivan Toney seen as more of a wildcard to use in specific situations. “I think Ollie is more the guy we need to start for Harry, if we think Harry should not start a match,” he said. “He can keep the intensity up, to keep the press going.

“Ivan is kind of a finisher for us. Maybe it’s a special task to take the attention off Harry. Then we have a second striker who’s very, very good in the box. He’s a good penalty taker. He trains on a high level. I’m very happy with him. He just showed that it was right to take him. He has a brilliant attitude. We have some options but Harry is, of course, the main guy in front.”

Tuchel downplayed concerns over the state of the pitch in Tampa, which is home to the NFL’s Tampa Bay Buccaneers. “We have a greenkeeper who takes care of it and I hope it will be all right,” he said. “It is an American football pitch. We are told it is OK. I saw just a photo, that made me a little bit worried but let’s decide when we are there.”

England’s final friendly is against Costa Rica in Orlando on Wednesday. They do not play their first game in Group L until facing Croatia in Dallas on 15 June, giving them time to adjust to the hot weather. The squad’s Arsenal contingent will not be involved against New Zealand, having been given permission to arrive in Florida late after last weekend’s Champions League final.

Anthony Head, Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Ted Lasso actor, dies aged 72

The Guardian Fri, 05 Jun 2026 19:33:35 GMT

British actor starred on the West End before finding international fame in the 90s on Buffy the Vampire Slayer

Anthony Head brought gravitas to Buffy and everything else he touched

Anthony Head, the actor best-known for playing Rupert Giles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, has died aged 72.

“He passed away peacefully of complications due to pneumonia, surrounded by his family,” his daughters Emily and Daisy Head said in a statement.

“It has been, and forever will be, an honour and a privilege to be his daughters, and to have witnessed first-hand the impact both he and his work have had on so many.”

As well as playing the mentor to Sarah Michelle Gellar’s character, Head had a recurring role in David Walliams and Matt Lucas’s BBC sketch show Little Britain, appeared in the BBC production of Merlin as well as film roles in The Iron Lady and The Inbetweeners Movie. More recently, he played former football club owner Rupert Mannion in Ted Lasso.

Gellar began her Instagram tribute to Head with a quote from her Buffy character: “Tell Giles I figured it out and I’m ok”

“Well I don’t have it figured out and I’m not ok,” she continued. “But I know I’m the lucky one because I knew you. Thank you to Daisy and Emily who not only shared their dad with me, but with the world.

Born in Camden, London, Head was raised by artistic parents. His father was a documentary film-maker who founded Verity Films, while his mother was an actor who played Madame Maigret in the 60s BBC crime drama Maigret. Meanwhile his brother was also an actor best known for his lead role in 1971’s Sunday Bloody Sunday.

The Head family were committed to the arts and imparted their passion to their son. “My Christmas present was always a new dressing-up outfit that my mother – who was a brilliant seamstress – would make herself,” Head told the Guardian in 2016.

“At playgroup the woman who ran it took my parents aside one day and said, we love it when Anthony comes in dressing-up clothes, but it would be really nice to meet Anthony himself one day – he gets absolutely immersed in whatever character he’s dressed up as.”

Head began his professional career on the stage, starring in the 1978 West End revival of Godspell alongside Su Pollard. In the following decade, he took on various projects, including a role in the 1981 adaptation of Lady Chatterley’s Lover and a part in 1987’s A Prayer for the Dying alongside Bob Hoskins and Liam Neeson.

In the early 80s, Head also sang backing vocals for the British pop group Red Box, and was featured on their 1986 debut album The Circle & the Square. He was arguably best known in the UK and US for his role in Nescafé’s Gold Blend TV adverts, which focused on the slow-burn courtship between a British couple.

Yet the stage remained Head’s focus, with a lead role as Freddie Trumper in the original West End production of the Abba musical Chess in 1988, as well as performing in productions of A Patriot for Me and Lady Windermere’s Fan. He also took a starring role as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the 1990 West End production of The Rocky Horror Show.

After winning the role of Giles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Head moved to Los Angeles for five years while his partner, Sarah, and two young daughters lived in England.

“I’d try to go home to them every three or four weeks,” he told the Guardian. “The production team would work dates around me, and every time I got the chance to have six days clear, I’d get on a plane … I spent quite a lot of money on airfares, but we made it work.”

Head said that his rise to global fame taught him “not to get caught up in the hype. [Co-stars] Alyson Hannigan and Sarah Michelle Gellar would talk about magazine covers, and I’d think: where’s mine? They were competing, but ultimately it’s a game that only lasts so long. It’s better to just get on with the job.”

After Buffy the Vampire Slayer ended in 2003, Head took a recurring role in Little Britain. The actor played a British prime minister who is constantly fawned over by a flirtatious assistant (Walliams).

In Ted Lasso, he regularly featured in scenes with the show co-creator Jason Sudeikis, with the pair praised for their intuitive on-screen chemistry.

“We know how dearly he will be missed by friends, colleagues and fans of the shows he was in – he loved his job very much and he always considered himself incredibly lucky to have been able to work alongside such exceptionally talented people, in such wonderful productions, across a career that spanned several decades,” said his daughters.

“Our grief is far greater than the hole he has left behind but we know his legacy will live on in the shows he was a part of and in the audiences that love them.

“How lucky we are to know we are able to watch him doing what he loved, even when he is no longer with us.”

Head’s partner, Sarah Fisher, died in December 2025, aged 61. “It is immensely shocking to us all, and came with very little warning. No words could ever express all that she encompassed, or begin to describe the crater her absence has left,” the couple’s daughters said in a statement at the time.

Tributes have also been pouring in from those who knew and worked with Head.

“I am very sad indeed to learn of the passing of Tony Head,” the Little Britain co-creator Matt Lucas wrote on X. “When we were casting Little Britain, we were looking for a ‘Tony Head-type’, because we never imagined for a moment that the man himself would be interested, but he was. Lucky us. He was unfailingly brilliant, and always so kind and warm. My heart goes out to Daisy and Emily.”

“He was so kind and generous of a soul,” wrote Head’s Buffy the Vampire Slayer co-star David Boreanaz on Instagram.

“There’s a hole in the world,” said James Marsters, who played Spike in the TV show. “Anthony Head has passed on from us. He was an unflaggingly kind and steady presence on the set of Buffy, and the best actor in the cast. He was the best of us. I was lucky to have known, and learned from him. He left the world a better place for his presence. Thank you Tony for all you gave.”

“Tony H – for every scene and time shared, I give thanks,” said Buffy co-star Eliza Dushku. “Rest in love and peace, kind sir. A dear one.”

“Anthony Head was a brilliant actor who played the worst person in the world, which was an incredible skill because he was the best person,” said Head’s Ted Lasso co-star Brett Goldstein on Instagram Stories. “Infinitely charming and kind and fun and a joy. He will be sorely missed. Love to his family.”

Starmer suggests US ‘trying to interfere in our democracy’ over Nowak claims

The Guardian Fri, 05 Jun 2026 19:12:07 GMT

Prime minister’s office responds after JD Vance blames British teenager’s death on mass migration

How Britain was rocked by Henry Nowak’s murder – and why the US intervened

​Keir Starmer has suggested the US is trying to interfere in British democracy after JD Vance, the US vice-president, blamed the murder of the British teenager Henry Nowak on mass migration.

The prime minister’s office responded after the senior Republican politician claimed in a post on X that Nowak would be alive “if the last few generations of European elites had stood their ground against the politics of self-hatred and the mass invasion of migrants, many of whom despise the West and the people who love it”.

Downing Street did not name Vance directly but said its response to his comments was that “in recent days we have seen people trying to interfere in our democracy and seeking to stir up division on our streets”.

“The Nowak family are grieving after Henry’s horrific murder. They have said they do not want his death to be used to create further division, hatred or tension. We should be respecting their wishes,” a spokesperson said.

“Our politics should bring people together even in the most terrible of circumstances. That is who we are as a country.”

There has been a national outcry about Nowak’s murder as footage showed police officers handcuffed him as he lay dying from stab wounds after his killer, Vickrum Digwa, had falsely accused him of racist abuse. Digwa, a British-born Sikh, was ultimately convicted of murder and jailed for life with a minimum of 21 years.

Nowak’s family, who met Starmer on Thursday, asked that his death not be used to create further division, hatred or tension. But since the conviction, rightwing US figures have made several remarks about the case. The US state department, run by Marco Rubio, portrayed the case as an example of the UK’s “civilisational decline”.

In a post on X, the department said: “Ideological conditioning and two-tiered policing are glaring symptoms of civilizational decline. They must be rejected across the West. The United States sends our condolences to the family of Henry Nowak and the people of the United Kingdom at this troubling time.”

Subsequently, Starmer said the police’s response was under review but rejected the US state department’s characterisation of UK policing. He told LBC: “It is really important that we are very, very clear, policing without fear or favour, whatever anybody else says, and wherever they’re saying it from, whichever country in the world.” He also said the UK must not shy away from asking difficult questions of the police.

The Liberal Democrats have called for the US ambassador to the UK to be summoned over what they called “flagrant foreign interference that seeks to fan the flames of division”. The party’s leader, Ed Davey, said the Trump administration was “attacking our democracy, not in secret, but openly on social media”.

“Starmer needs to show some backbone and call this out today. We can’t turn a blind eye to this blatant interference any longer,” Davey said.

No 10, however, said the relationship with the US remained “incredibly strong” despite the difference of view on policing. It declined to be drawn on whether the US would be rebuked in any diplomatic conversations.

Nowak’s murder has been claimed by some as evidence of two-tier policing in the UK – the argument that some groups of people are dealt with more harshly than others for ideological reasons.

The owner of X, Elon Musk, and the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, are among those to have claimed the circumstances of Nowak’s death in Southampton were evidence of bias against white people. Both have in turn been accused of exploiting the teenager’s death.

David Lammy, the UK’s deputy prime minister, told Sky News on Friday that he welcomed the US government’s condolences to the Nowak family but said he did not recognise “this caricature of Britain having a two-tier criminal justice system”.

Starmer on Thursday accused Musk of “interfering in our politics” and attempting to create division.

Musk is a regular poster of ethnonationalist content and a supporter of Restore Britain, the far-right party set up by Rupert Lowe, a former Reform MP. He has posted for weeks on his social media platform about Nowak’s murder, often using far-right themes and talking points.

The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct, is examining the behaviour of the officers who handcuffed Nowak after he had been fatally stabbed.

Starmer met Nowak’s family at Downing Street on Thursday to discuss a response to the actions of Hampshire police, saying afterwards he had promised to take “whatever action is required to right the wrongs in this case”.
